title: Operators, Control Flow & Type Conversion
intro: Operators and expressions, decision making, loops, jump statements and implicit versus explicit type conversion.

sec.s: C is a procedural programming language.

b.x: C is a procedural programming language. A C program is built from declarations, expressions, statements, functions, and blocks. An expression computes a value or performs an operation that may have a side effect. A statement tells the program to do something, such as assign a value, choose a branch, repeat a block, or transfer control elsewhere. For example:
The expression “12 + 8” computes 20. The declaration initializes total with that value. In the statement:

the relational expression “total >= 20” is tested. In C, a condition is false when its value compares equal to zero and true when it is nonzero. This differs from languages that require a separate Boolean type in every condition. C has the type _Bool in C99 and later, and the header <stdbool.h> provides the convenient name bool, plus true and false, but ordinary integer expressions can still be used as conditions.

Control flow is the order in which statements execute. Normally, statements run in sequence from top to bottom. Decision statements choose a path; loops repeat statements; jump statements alter the normal path. Operators build the expressions that decisions and loops test. Consider:

The operator >= compares age with 18. Its result is an integer value of 1 if the comparison is true and 0 if false. The if statement then chooses one block. Understanding operators, expressions, and control flow together is therefore more useful than memorizing each topic in isolation. Throughout these notes, examples use standard C syntax. Include the necessary headers, such as <stdio.h> for printf and scanf.

A complete program should usually define int main(void) or int main(int argc, char **argv), and return an int status. Do not confuse C with C++: some syntax and conversion rules differ between the languages.

sec.s: An operator is a symbol that requests an operation on one or more operands.

b.x: An operator is a symbol that requests an operation on one or more operands. An operand is the value or expression on which the operator works. For example, in “a + b”, plus is the operator and a and b are operands. Operators are often classified by how many operands they take:

x: Binary operators take two operands: a + b, x < y, p && q.
The conditional operator ?: uses three expressions and is commonly called the ternary operator.

b.x: The main operator groups in this syllabus are arithmetic, relational, logical, assignment, bitwise, and conditional. Increment/decrement, sizeof, address and pointer operators are also important in C, although they are not the primary focus here.

sec.s: Arithmetic operators perform mathematical operations on numeric values.

b.x: Arithmetic operators perform mathematical operations on numeric values.

Addition, subtraction, and multiplication work with arithmetic types. The type of the result depends on the types of the operands and the usual arithmetic conversions. The simple examples below use int values.

Integer division discards the fractional part toward zero. Thus 17 / 5 is 3, not 3.4. Likewise, -17 / 5 is -3 in modern standard C, because truncation is toward zero. If a floating-point result is required, at least one operand must be floating point:
The % operator calculates a remainder and is used with integer operands, not floating-point operands. For example, 17 % 5 is 2. A common use is testing divisibility:

If number is divisible by 2, its remainder is zero. The same technique can test multiples of 3, 5, or another nonzero integer. Do not use a zero divisor with / or %: that causes undefined behavior. Signed integer overflow is also undefined behavior in C; do not assume that a very large int will wrap around safely. Unsigned arithmetic, by contrast, wraps modulo one more than its maximum representable value.
Operator precedence matters. Multiplication and division bind more tightly than addition and subtraction:
Parentheses make the intended grouping explicit. For code that matters, prefer readable parentheses over forcing the reader to remember every precedence level. Common arithmetic mistakes:

x: Writing a = b / c when b and c are int and expecting decimals.
Dividing or taking remainder by zero.
Forgetting that a variable’s type can limit the result range.
Mixing signed and unsigned integers without understanding conversion.
Assuming an expression such as x + y changes x. It does not; assignment or a side-effect operator is needed to modify a variable.
Using a comparison where assignment was intended, or vice versa.

b.x: A compound statement such as:
does not alter length or width. It calculates their product and stores the result in area.

sec.s: Relational operators compare two values.

b.x: Relational operators compare two values. Their result is 1 when true and 0 when false.
Examples:
The equality operator is ==, with two equals signs. A single = is assignment. This is one of the most frequent beginner errors:

In C, an assignment expression has a value, so writing if (score = 50) is usually legal but likely wrong: it assigns 50 to score and the resulting nonzero value makes the condition true. Compilers commonly warn about this. When an assignment inside a condition is intentional, make the intention obvious and heed compiler warnings. Relational comparisons can be combined with logical operators. For example:

This checks both endpoints. Do not write mathematical chained comparisons like “18 <= age <= 60” expecting the same result as in mathematics. C parses that as “(18 <= age) <= 60”. The first comparison becomes 0 or 1, and both values are less than or equal to 60, so the whole expression is usually true. Write two comparisons connected by && instead. For floating-point numbers, equality tests require care.

Floating-point values often cannot represent decimal fractions exactly. For example, repeated calculations intended to produce 0.3 might yield a nearby representable value. When approximate equality is appropriate, compare the absolute difference against a chosen tolerance, such as fabs(a - b) < 1e-9, after including <math.h> and selecting a tolerance suitable for the problem’s scale.
This is not a universal tolerance; measurement units and expected error matter. Relational operators are especially useful in if statements and loop tests:
The loop continues while count is less than 10. If the condition is initially false, a while loop executes zero times.

sec.s: Logical operators combine or reverse truth values.

b.x: Logical operators combine or reverse truth values. In C, zero means false and any nonzero scalar value used as a condition means true.
Logical AND (&&) is true only if both operands are true. Logical OR (||) is true if at least one operand is true. Logical NOT (!) reverses truth: !0 is 1, and !nonzero is 0. Truth table:

x: A  B  |  A && B  |  A || B

b.x: For NOT:

The table uses 0 and 1 for simplicity. In C, operands need not literally be 0 or 1; logical operators produce 0 or 1. Short-circuit evaluation is a crucial feature. For A && B, if A is false, C does not evaluate B because the whole result must be false. For A || B, if A is true, C does not evaluate B because the whole result must be true. This behavior is useful for safe guards:
If denominator is zero, the division is not evaluated. Reversing the order could attempt division by zero. Another example:

x: if (ptr != NULL && *ptr == 'A') { /* safe to dereference ptr if it is a valid pointer or NULL */ }

b.x: The check protects against NULL, but it cannot prove that every non-NULL pointer is valid. A dangling or otherwise invalid pointer remains unsafe. Use logical operators for conditions, not bitwise operators by accident. “&&” is logical AND, whereas “&” is bitwise AND. “||” is logical OR, whereas “|” is bitwise OR. Logical operators reduce their result to 0 or 1 and have short-circuit behavior.
Bitwise operators act on individual bits and evaluate their operands according to ordinary expression rules. Examples:

Avoid relying on obscure side effects inside logical expressions. While short-circuiting is defined, compact expressions that both modify variables and test them are harder to understand. Clear, separate statements are often safer.

sec.s: Assignment stores a value in a modifiable object.

b.x: Assignment stores a value in a modifiable object. The basic operator is =.

The left operand must be a modifiable lvalue, such as an ordinary variable. You cannot assign to a literal like 10 = points. In C, an assignment expression also has a value, but using assignments as part of complicated expressions can make code confusing. Compound assignment combines an operation with assignment:
Examples:
Compound assignment can make updates concise, especially in counters and accumulators:

There is a subtle difference between compound assignment and spelling out the long form when the left expression has side effects. In “array[i++] += 5”, the left side is evaluated only once. Rewriting it carelessly as “array[i++] = array[i++] + 5” evaluates i++ more than once and can produce different or undefined behavior.
For simple variables, the two forms usually express the same intended update, subject to conversion details. Assignment is right-associative:

This is grouped as a = (b = (c = 10)), so c is assigned 10, then b, then a. Although legal, multiple assignments in one statement should be used only when they improve clarity. Remember that “int a = 5;” is initialization in a declaration, while “a = 5;” is assignment after the variable exists. Assignment conversions can change the value. For example:

x: n = 3.9;  // n becomes 3 after conversion to int

b.x: The fractional part is discarded when converting a finite floating-point value to an integer, provided the truncated value is representable. If the result is outside the representable range, behavior is undefined for the floating-to-integer conversion. Do not use implicit conversion as a substitute for explicit validation when values come from user input.

sec.s: Bitwise operators operate on the individual bits of integer operands.

b.x: Bitwise operators operate on the individual bits of integer operands. They are used in flags, masks, embedded systems, low-level programming, compact data representations, and some performance-sensitive tasks.

Use unsigned integer types when reasoning about bit patterns is important. Bitwise operations on signed values can be surprising, and right-shifting a negative signed integer has implementation-defined behavior in traditional C standards. Shift counts must be nonnegative and less than the width of the promoted left operand; invalid shift counts cause undefined behavior.

Left shifting a signed value can also be undefined in cases where the result is not representable. These rules make unsigned operands the clearer choice for bit manipulation. For a simple 4-bit example, consider a = 1100 and b = 1010. These are binary representations, not decimal numbers. Bitwise AND (&): a bit is 1 only when both corresponding bits are 1.
Bitwise OR (|): a bit is 1 when at least one corresponding bit is 1.
Bitwise XOR (^): a bit is 1 when the corresponding bits differ.

Bitwise complement (~) flips each bit in the integer representation. The result depends on the width and type of the operand and on integer promotions, so avoid claiming that ~5 is always a particular decimal number on every implementation. For unsigned types of a known width, its behavior is easier to reason about. Shift operators move bits left or right:

x: unsigned int left = x << 1;  // binary ...00001010, value 10
unsigned int right = x >> 1;  // binary ...00000010, value 2

b.x: For unsigned values, shifting left by one is equivalent to multiplication by 2 only when the result is interpreted within the type’s width and no relevant bits are lost; shifting right by one corresponds to division by 2 rounded down. Do not assume that shifts are a universally safe replacement for arithmetic, especially for signed values. A common use is a bit mask.
Suppose bit 0 represents “enabled”, bit 1 represents “read permission”, and bit 2 represents “write permission”:

The pattern “(flags & mask) != 0” tests whether any selected bit is set. The expression “flags |= mask” sets selected bits. The expression “flags &= ~mask” clears selected bits. The expression “flags ^= mask” toggles selected bits. These patterns are common in firmware and hardware-related code, but their use should be documented because bit masks can be less obvious than ordinary Boolean variables.
Bitwise AND and logical AND are not interchangeable:

x: a && b  // 1, because both are nonzero a & b
// 0, because binary 0010 AND 0100 has no set bits

b.x: Likewise, a | b computes a bitwise combination, while a || b returns 1 if either operand is nonzero. Bitwise operators do not short-circuit.

sec.s: The conditional operator ?: is C’s only standard operator that takes three operands, so it is often…

b.x: The conditional operator ?: is C’s only standard operator that takes three operands, so it is often called the ternary operator. Its general form is:
The condition is evaluated first. If it is nonzero, the second expression is evaluated; otherwise, the third expression is evaluated. Only one of those two result expressions is evaluated. Example:
maximum becomes 12. This is a compact alternative to:
Another example:
The conditional operator is useful when choosing one of two values. It can also be used inside a return expression:

This example works for ordinary negative values, but note that negating the most negative representable signed integer can overflow; robust general code must account for the range of int. Avoid nesting many conditional operators:

x: result = a > b ? (a > c ? a : c) : (b > c ? b : c);

b.x: This may be valid, but an if-else structure is usually easier to read. The conditional operator is an expression, while if-else is a statement. Use ?: to select a value, not to cram a long program into one line. The condition is evaluated once, and only one branch expression is evaluated. That allows code such as:
The division occurs only when divisor is nonzero. Still, when safety matters, a normal if statement can make the guard easier to inspect.

sec.s: The increment operator ++ adds one to a modifiable scalar object.

b.x: The increment operator ++ adds one to a modifiable scalar object. The decrement operator -- subtracts one.
Both prefix and postfix forms exist:

x: ++x: increment x, and the expression’s value is the value after increment.
x++: the expression’s value is the value before increment; x is then incremented as a side effect. - --x and x-- follow the analogous rule.

b.x: Example:

x: int a = ++x;  // x is 5; a is 5
int b = y++;  // b is 4; y is 5

b.x: In a loop header, “i++” is common and usually straightforward. In complex expressions, combining multiple modifications to the same object can create undefined behavior or unclear code. Avoid expressions such as “i = i++” and “printf("%d %d", i++, i++)”; the relative evaluation of function arguments is not specified in the way beginners often expect, and unsequenced modifications can invoke undefined behavior.
Prefer separate statements.

sec.s: Precedence determines how operators are grouped when parentheses are absent.

b.x: Precedence determines how operators are grouped when parentheses are absent. Associativity determines grouping when operators of the same precedence appear together. Neither concept, by itself, tells you the order in which every subexpression is evaluated. A useful partial precedence list, from higher to lower, is:

x: Postfix: function call (), array indexing [], member access ., ->, postfix ++ and --.
Unary: prefix ++ and --, unary + and -, !, ~, casts, sizeof, &, *.

b.x: This is a simplified list of the operators most relevant to these notes. Other operators such as pointer/member operations fit into the full C precedence table. When in doubt, consult a reliable C reference and add parentheses. Examples:

x: a = b = c = 7;  // assignment groups right-to-left

b.x: The expression: if (a < b && b < c) is clearer than relying on implicit assumptions. Parentheses can improve clarity even when they are not required:

A major distinction: precedence controls grouping, not general evaluation order. For example, in “f() + g()”, precedence says addition combines the results of f and g, but it does not generally guarantee whether f() or g() runs first. Do not write code that depends on an unspecified evaluation order.

Logical && and || have special sequencing and short-circuit rules; the comma operator also sequences its left operand before its right operand. The comma that separates function arguments or declarations is not the comma operator.

sec.s: Decision-making statements let a program select which statements to execute based on a condition or…

b.x: Decision-making statements let a program select which statements to execute based on a condition or selector value. They implement branching logic such as validating input, assigning grades, granting access, choosing menu actions, and handling errors.

sec.s: The if statement executes a statement or block only when its controlling expression is nonzero.

b.x: The if statement executes a statement or block only when its controlling expression is nonzero. Syntax:
Example:

If temperature is 35, the condition is true and the message prints. If temperature is 25, the condition is false and the block is skipped. Braces are not strictly required for a single statement, but using braces consistently reduces errors:

This is legal, but the braced version is safer when adding another statement. Indentation does not determine which statements belong to the if; braces do. A condition can use a variable, comparison, logical expression, or function call. Examples:

x: if (count) { ... }  // true if count is nonzero

b.x: For beginner code, explicit comparisons often improve readability. A function used in a condition should have a clear return meaning and should not have surprising side effects.

sec.s: Use if-else when exactly one of two paths should be chosen.

b.x: Use if-else when exactly one of two paths should be chosen. Syntax:
Example:
Since 9 % 2 is 1, the else block executes. Only one branch runs. If both branches contain several statements, braces are essential for clarity. A practical validation example:

x: printf("You are below the required age.\n");

b.x: This example demonstrates the control structure, not a complete legal or identity verification system. Real applications should validate all relevant requirements rather than relying on a single value. The “dangling else” rule can confuse beginners. In nested if statements, an else is associated with the nearest preceding if that does not already have an else. Braces remove ambiguity and should be preferred.

sec.s: An else-if ladder checks multiple alternatives in order.

b.x: An else-if ladder checks multiple alternatives in order. The first true condition’s block runs; later conditions are skipped.

Order matters. If “marks >= 40” appeared first, a mark of 95 would satisfy that first condition and later grades would never be checked. Arrange conditions from the most specific/highest threshold to the more general ones, or otherwise design the order deliberately. Boundary testing is important. For the example above, test marks 39, 40, 59, 60, 74, 75, 89, 90, and 100.

Decide what should happen for invalid values such as -5 or 120, and add validation if necessary. An else branch handles all values that fail previous conditions, including invalid ones unless separate checks are included.

sec.s: A nested if is an if statement placed inside another if or else block.

b.x: A nested if is an if statement placed inside another if or else block. It is useful when a later test should be performed only after an earlier condition is satisfied. Example:

The outer if checks age. Only when age is at least 18 does the inner if test identification. The code expresses a dependency: the second test is relevant only after the first condition passes. A nested structure can become difficult to follow when too many levels are added.

Alternatives include combining independent conditions with &&, using an else-if ladder, extracting logic into a function, or returning early from a function after invalid input. Do not combine conditions automatically: nested if is sometimes clearer when the second test must not be evaluated unless the first test succeeds. A more realistic example:

This illustrates branching only. Authentication systems should not store plain-text passwords or reveal sensitive details in ways that enable account enumeration. In production code, use secure password hashing, rate limits, and carefully designed error messages.

sec.s: switch is useful when one integer-like selector is compared against several constant alternatives.

b.x: switch is useful when one integer-like selector is compared against several constant alternatives. It often makes menu selection clearer than a long else-if ladder. General form:

In standard C, the controlling expression has an integer type after the integer promotions, or an enumeration type. Each case label must be an integer constant expression, and case values must be unique. You cannot use arbitrary strings or floating-point values as case labels in standard C. Example:

When choice is 2, execution jumps to case 2, prints “Open file”, then break exits the switch. If no case matches, default runs if it exists. default is optional, but including it is often a good way to handle unexpected values. The break statements are important because switch has fall-through behavior.
If a case finishes without break, execution continues into the statements under the next case label until a break or the end of the switch is reached.
If option is 1, this prints both One and Two. That may be intentional, but often it is a bug. If fall-through is deliberate, document it clearly. Multiple case labels can share a block:

Here both 6 and 7 lead to the same statement. Validate day separately if values outside 1 through 7 must be rejected; otherwise the default message may incorrectly label an invalid day as a weekday. A switch is not a replacement for every conditional. It does not directly express arbitrary ranges such as “score >= 80”, nor does it compare strings in standard C.
Use if/else for ranges, complex logical conditions, and floating-point comparisons. Use switch for discrete constant choices.

sec.s: Both can implement the same logic in some cases.

b.x: Use if/else when:

x: Conditions involve ranges, such as marks >= 80.
Conditions combine several comparisons, such as age >= 18 && has_id.
The values are floating-point or strings requiring custom comparison.
Conditions need a sequence of related tests. Use switch when:
One selector is compared against a set of discrete integer or enum values.
Each choice maps to a distinct action.
A menu or command code is being handled.
Shared case blocks make the alternatives easier to read.

b.x: Both can implement the same logic in some cases. The best choice is the one that communicates intent clearly and correctly. Good control flow is not measured by the fewest lines of code.

sec.s: A loop repeats a statement or block while a condition or iteration rule allows it.

b.x: A loop repeats a statement or block while a condition or iteration rule allows it. Loops are useful for processing arrays, reading records, repeating menus, counting, searching, calculating totals, and handling input. A loop usually needs:
If the condition never becomes false and no jump exits the loop, it may be infinite. Infinite loops are sometimes intentional, such as an event loop, but accidental infinite loops are a common bug.

sec.s: The condition is checked before each iteration.

b.x: Syntax:
The condition is checked before each iteration. If it is false initially, the body runs zero times. Example:
The steps are:

x: When i becomes 6, the condition is false and the loop ends.

b.x: The update is essential. Omitting i++ in this example means i remains 1, so the condition remains true and the program prints 1 forever. Sometimes the update occurs inside the body conditionally, but every possible path should be checked to ensure the loop can make progress.
A while loop is often best when the number of repetitions is not known in advance, such as reading until a sentinel value or waiting for valid input. Example: sum numbers from 1 through n.

At the end, sum is 15. The accumulator starts at zero because zero is the identity value for addition. The loop invariant is that after processing i values, sum contains the total of the numbers already processed. Thinking about invariants helps detect off-by-one errors. Example: sentinel-controlled loop:

The condition checks whether scanf successfully read an integer before using value. The input value 0 is the sentinel and is not added. In real programs, handle invalid input carefully: if scanf fails because the next input is not an integer, the stream may need to be cleaned or the program should report an error. Input validation is separate from the loop syntax but essential to robust behavior.

sec.s: A do-while loop checks its condition after executing the body.

b.x: A do-while loop checks its condition after executing the body. Therefore, the body runs at least once. Syntax:
Notice the semicolon after the closing parenthesis. Forgetting it is a syntax error. Example:
This prints 1 through 5, similar to the previous while example. The difference becomes clear when the condition is false at the beginning:
Even though x < 5 is false, the body has already executed once. With a while loop, the same body would not execute at all. A do-while loop is suitable for a menu that must display at least once:

This is an illustrative example; a production menu should also deal with non-numeric input in a way that does not repeatedly fail on the same input. The main point is that the menu appears before the exit condition is tested. Choose do-while when the operation must happen once before deciding whether to repeat. Choose while when the condition must be checked before the first execution.

sec.s: The for loop groups initialization, condition, and update in one header.

b.x: The for loop groups initialization, condition, and update in one header. Syntax:
Example:
In C99 and later, declaring int i in the for initializer is valid, and i’s scope is limited to the loop. In older C dialects, declare i before the loop. Execution order:
The semicolons inside the header separate its three parts. They are not interchangeable with commas. The update may be i++, i += 2, or another expression. A for loop can also omit one or more parts:

This is valid but a conventional while loop may be clearer. A loop with all three parts omitted, for (;;) { … }, is an infinite loop unless it exits using break, return, goto, or another control-flow mechanism. Example: print even numbers from 2 through 10.
Example: calculate factorial iteratively.

For n = 5, the result is 120. The cast documents the intended conversion but does not magically prevent overflow; unsigned long long has a finite range. For larger factorials, use a suitable big-integer library or stop before the result exceeds the type’s maximum. Validate that n is nonnegative and within a supported range. A for loop is usually appropriate when the iteration variable and number of steps are clear.
A while loop often communicates a condition-driven process more naturally. This is a style choice, not a strict rule.

sec.s: A nested loop is a loop inside another loop.

b.x: A nested loop is a loop inside another loop. For each iteration of the outer loop, the inner loop runs through its own iterations. Nested loops are common for grids, tables, matrices, patterns, and pairwise comparisons. Example: a 3-by-4 grid of stars.

The outer loop selects the row. The inner loop prints four stars for each row. The newline is after the inner loop, so it runs once per row. If the newline were inside the inner loop, every star would appear on a separate line. Example: multiplication table.
The format specifier %4d reserves a field width of four characters, helping columns align. The product i * j is calculated for each pair. Example: lower-left triangle.

Nested loops can have different variables and conditions. Avoid reusing the same counter variable for both loops unless the design specifically requires it; changing the outer loop’s counter inside the inner loop can break the logic. The approximate number of body executions in a rectangular nested loop is the product of the iteration counts.

If an outer loop runs n times and the inner loop runs m times each time, the inner body executes n × m times. This helps estimate runtime. For example, comparing every element against every other element often requires quadratic work, O(n^2), while processing a simple array once is usually O(n). Big-O notation is a separate topic, but nested-loop structure is one of its most visible introductory examples.
Example: print pairs of distinct numbers from 1 to 3:
This creates ordered pairs where i and j differ. If only unique unordered pairs are needed, use j = i + 1 as the inner initialization.

sec.s: An infinite loop has a condition that never becomes false or is deliberately written to continue…

b.x: An infinite loop has a condition that never becomes false or is deliberately written to continue indefinitely.

This can be valid in embedded systems and servers, but the program must have a defined exit strategy where appropriate. An accidental infinite loop may be caused by a missing update, a condition that can never be false, or updating the wrong variable. To design a loop:

x: Write a condition that describes when more work remains.
Ensure each iteration makes progress toward stopping.
Check boundary values: zero, one, maximum, and invalid inputs.
Decide what should happen if input or a function call fails.
Use braces and descriptive variable names.
Test a small example manually before using a large dataset.

b.x: Off-by-one errors are particularly common. Compare i < n with i <= n:

x: i++ executes n times for positive n. - i = 1;
i++ also executes n times for positive n. - i = 0;

b.x: i++ executes n + 1 times. The correct form depends on whether values are zero-based indices or one-based counts.

sec.s: Jump statements transfer control rather than simply continuing to the next statement.

b.x: Jump statements transfer control rather than simply continuing to the next statement. The main statements here are break, continue, and goto. The return statement is also a control transfer from a function, although it has a different purpose.

sec.s: break immediately exits the nearest enclosing loop or switch statement.

b.x: break immediately exits the nearest enclosing loop or switch statement. Execution resumes at the statement after that loop or switch. Example:
When i becomes 6, break exits the for loop. The update expression is not executed after break; control leaves the loop immediately. break is useful when:

x: A search finds the target and no more scanning is needed.
A sentinel or special condition requires early exit.
A menu’s exit option should end a switch or loop.
A validation or error condition makes further iterations unnecessary.

b.x: Example: linear search.

The break avoids checking later elements after the target is found. In nested loops, break exits only the innermost loop or switch, not every enclosing loop. To leave multiple nested loops, consider a helper function with return, a carefully designed flag, or another clear structure rather than scattering jumps throughout the code. Remember that break inside switch exits the switch, not necessarily an outer loop.
For example, a break in a switch nested inside a for loop ends the switch and the for loop continues unless another break is reached in the outer loop.

sec.s: continue skips the remainder of the current iteration of the nearest enclosing loop and proceeds to…

b.x: continue skips the remainder of the current iteration of the nearest enclosing loop and proceeds to the next iteration. It does not terminate the loop itself. It applies to loops, not switch statements by themselves. Example:
When i is even, continue skips printf. The loop still performs its update and checks the next condition. The exact next step depends on the loop type:

x: In a for loop, continue proceeds to the update expression, then the condition is tested.
In a while loop, continue proceeds to the condition test.
In a do-while loop, continue proceeds to the condition test at the bottom.

b.x: This difference matters if the update is written inside a while-loop body. For example, a while loop that uses continue before updating its counter can become infinite:

x: continue;  // bug: i never changes from 2

b.x: When i reaches 2, the loop continually continues without incrementing i. A corrected design moves the update before the continue, changes the structure, or uses a for loop where the update occurs automatically after continue:

This prints 0, 1, 3, and 4. Use continue when skipping an item is a normal part of the loop’s logic, such as ignoring invalid records or processing only values meeting a condition. Do not use it so heavily that the main work becomes difficult to follow.

sec.s: goto transfers control to a labeled statement within the same function.

b.x: goto transfers control to a labeled statement within the same function. Syntax:

The label is an identifier followed by a colon. A goto cannot jump directly to a label in another function. It can jump forward or backward within the same function, subject to the language’s rules. A small example:
The goto jumps to finished, so the first printf does not execute. This example demonstrates syntax, not a recommendation to use goto for ordinary branching. Why goto is usually discouraged:

x: It can make the path through a function difficult to follow.
A jump backward can accidentally create a loop.
Many jumps can produce tangled “spaghetti code.”
Structured constructs such as if, for, while, break, and return are usually clearer.

b.x: There are limited situations where goto can be useful in C, particularly for centralized cleanup when a function acquires several resources and any later operation may fail. For example, a function might allocate memory, open a file, then encounter an error. A cleanup label can release resources in the correct order.
This pattern should still be carefully structured and should not be used as an excuse for arbitrary jumps. Illustrative cleanup pattern:

x: /* Perform work using file and buffer. */

b.x: This snippet requires <stdio.h> and <stdlib.h>. In real code, every resource must be initialized before cleanup can examine it, and cleanup must release only resources actually acquired. This is a common C pattern because C does not have automatic destructors like C++ objects. A simpler function may be better served by direct returns. Always choose the clearest correct structure.

sec.t: break, continue, goto, and return Compared
sec.s: continue skips nonpositive values.

x: exits the nearest enclosing loop or switch.
skips the rest of the current loop iteration.
jumps to a label within the current function.
exits the current function and optionally provides a return value.

b.x: Example:

x: int find_first_positive(const int values[], int count) {

sec.s: An expression is a combination of operands and operators that is evaluated according to C’s rules.

b.x: An expression is a combination of operands and operators that is evaluated according to C’s rules. It may produce a value, modify an object, call a function, or perform another side effect. Examples:

x: function_call(x) An expression can be used in a declaration initializer, an assignment, a condition, a function argument, a return statement, or as part of a larger expression.

b.x: Some expressions have no useful value but cause a side effect, such as a function call that prints a message. An expression followed by a semicolon is commonly an expression statement:
A declaration is not itself simply an expression. In “int x = 5;”, the declaration introduces x and initializes it; the initializer expression is 5.

sec.s: A side effect is a change to program state, such as modifying a variable, writing output, or…

b.x: A side effect is a change to program state, such as modifying a variable, writing output, or accessing a volatile object. Assignment and increment usually have side effects.

x: int y = x + 3;  // reads x, calculates 5; does not modify x

b.x: Avoid expressions that modify the same scalar object more than once without a sequencing relationship. For example, “i++ + i++” has undefined behavior in standard C because the modifications are unsequenced relative to each other. Its result is not something to memorize or predict. Similarly, the order of evaluating function arguments is not generally specified:

x: do not write this A clear alternative is: int first = i++;

b.x: Now the order is explicit.

sec.s: Precedence tells the compiler how to group operators.

b.x: Precedence tells the compiler how to group operators. Evaluation order tells when the parts are executed. These are different ideas. For example:

Precedence groups this as a + (b * c). It does not mean that the machine must evaluate b and c in a particular order before a. For ordinary pure arithmetic this distinction often does not affect the result, but it matters when function calls or side effects are involved. Logical && and || are special: their left operand is evaluated first, and the right operand is evaluated only if needed.

The comma operator evaluates its left operand before its right operand. Function arguments, however, should not be assumed to run left-to-right. Use temporary variables and separate statements whenever evaluation order matters. This is easier to debug, safer to maintain, and more portable.

sec.t: Integer Division, Remainder, and Common Pitfalls
sec.s: Integer division truncates toward zero.

b.x: Integer division truncates toward zero. Thus 9 / 4 is 2, while 9.0 / 4.0 is 2.25. If an integer result is assigned to a floating-point variable, the division may already have happened as integer division:

The type of the operands determines the arithmetic operation before the assignment conversion takes place. This is a fundamental principle: the destination type does not retroactively change the type of an expression. Remainder is often used for parity, cycles, and periodic behavior:

This is useful only when array_length is nonzero and the sign behavior is understood. For positive indices and positive lengths, the result is usually straightforward. If negative values are possible, define the intended normalization explicitly. Overflow and division:

x: Signed integer overflow is undefined behavior.
Division by zero is undefined behavior.
The special case of dividing the most negative signed integer by -1 may overflow and is undefined when the result cannot be represented.
A floating-point computation can lose precision or produce infinities or NaNs according to the implementation and floating-point environment.

b.x: When handling user input, validate ranges before arithmetic. Do not assume that checking after an overflowing operation can repair the problem.

sec.s: A type describes the kind of value an object can hold and the operations allowed on it.

b.x: A type describes the kind of value an object can hold and the operations allowed on it. Common arithmetic types include char, short, int, long, long long, their unsigned variants, float, double, and long double. C also has pointers, arrays, structures, unions, enumerations, and other types. A conversion changes a value from one type to another. C performs many conversions automatically; these are implicit conversions.

A programmer can also request a conversion using a cast; this is an explicit conversion. Conversion is not merely a spelling issue. It can change the numerical value, the range, precision, signedness, or interpretation of a value. Understanding when conversion occurs is essential for correct arithmetic and reliable input processing.

sec.s: Conversions are needed when different types interact.

b.x: Conversions are needed when different types interact. For example:

The int value 5 is converted to double, producing 5.0. This conversion is exact because every int value within the usual range can be represented exactly as a double on ordinary implementations, though the language’s type and representation guarantees should be distinguished from assumptions about every possible implementation. Conversions also happen in arithmetic:

The int operand x is converted to double so the addition can be performed using a common floating-point type. The result is 7.0. Conversions occur in assignment, function arguments, return statements, and conditional expressions. Integer promotions and the usual arithmetic conversions determine how operands are transformed before many operations.

sec.s: An implicit conversion is performed automatically by the language rules without a cast written by…

b.x: An implicit conversion is performed automatically by the language rules without a cast written by the programmer. Example 1: integer to floating point.
Example 2: floating point to integer.

For a finite floating value, conversion to an integer discards the fractional part toward zero if the truncated result is representable. This is not the same as rounding to the nearest integer. For rounding, use an appropriate function from <math.h>, such as round, lround, or nearbyint, according to the required behavior and result type. Example 3: mixed arithmetic.
quantity is converted to double for the multiplication, so total receives 7.5. Example 4: assignment to a narrower type.

This example explicitly casts, but it illustrates that storing a value in a type with a smaller range may change it. The exact range of unsigned char is implementation-defined in width, although it is guaranteed to have at least 8 bits. For an unsigned integer type, conversion is defined modulo one more than the maximum value of the destination type.

Do not assume a particular result for conversion to a signed type when the value is not representable; the rules depend on the relevant C standard and type. Implicit conversions are convenient but can hide bugs. For example, comparing a signed int with an unsigned int may convert the signed value to unsigned. A negative signed value can then become a very large unsigned value, making the comparison surprising.

x: if (a < b) { /* Do not assume this is true. */ }

b.x: On common systems, the usual arithmetic conversions convert a to unsigned int in this comparison, so the condition is false. The exact conversion rules depend on the types and their ranks, but the lesson is general: avoid mixing signed and unsigned values without a clear reason.

sec.t: Integer Promotions and Usual Arithmetic Conversions
sec.s: C performs integer promotions before many arithmetic and bitwise operations.

b.x: C performs integer promotions before many arithmetic and bitwise operations. Types such as char, signed char, unsigned char, short, and unsigned short are often promoted to int if int can represent every value of the original type; otherwise they are promoted to unsigned int. Enumeration types undergo related integer promotion rules. Example:

On a common system, both operands are promoted to int before addition, so the sum is 300. The result is then assigned to int. This explains why the operation is not necessarily performed in the narrow type just because the variables are narrow. The usual arithmetic conversions bring operands to a common type for many binary arithmetic operators.

Broadly: - If a floating-point operand participates, the other operand is converted as required to a compatible floating type. - Integer promotions occur first for integer types of lower rank. - If both operands are integer types, rank and signedness rules determine the common type. The exact rules are more detailed than this summary, especially for mixed signed and unsigned types.

The practical lesson is to use types that naturally fit the calculation, to avoid unnecessary mixing, and to use explicit conversions when the intended change is important and valid. For numerical code, think separately about:

x: The type used for the operation.
The type of the expression result.
The type of the destination. These may not all be the same.

sec.s: In an assignment, the right-hand value is converted to the type of the left-hand object before it…

b.x: In an assignment, the right-hand value is converted to the type of the left-hand object before it is stored, subject to the language’s rules.
The conversion occurs at assignment. Consider:
The division is integer division, so the result is 2, then converted to double as 2.0. To obtain 2.5:

A cast on one operand changes the arithmetic type used by the division. This is one of the most important practical examples of implicit versus explicit conversion. When assigning to a narrow integer type, check whether the value is in range. When assigning floating-point values to integers, decide whether truncation is acceptable.
When converting a signed value to unsigned, understand that a negative value maps to a value in the destination’s unsigned range rather than remaining negative.

sec.s: A cast requests a conversion explicitly.

b.x: A cast requests a conversion explicitly. The basic syntax is:
Examples:

A cast can document intent, but it does not make an invalid or dangerous conversion safe. Casting a large floating-point value to int does not solve an out-of-range problem. Casting away a pointer’s const qualification or converting unrelated pointer types can lead to undefined behavior or other problems if the resulting pointer is used incorrectly.
Use casts because the conversion is meaningful, not simply to silence compiler warnings. A good use of casting:

A poor habit is casting every expression without understanding why. For example, if both operands are already double, another cast is unnecessary. Likewise, a cast should not be used to hide a warning about an incompatible pointer or a suspicious signed/unsigned comparison. Investigate the cause. Explicit conversion is especially helpful when:

x: Integer division must become floating-point division.
A calculation should intentionally use a particular arithmetic type.
A value is deliberately narrowed after range checking.
A low-level bit operation requires an unsigned type.
A function or API expects a specific type and the conversion is valid.

sec.s: A narrowing conversion may lose information because the destination type cannot represent every…

b.x: A narrowing conversion may lose information because the destination type cannot represent every source value. Examples include double to float, double to int, long to int, or int to char. Whether the result is defined, implementation-defined, or undefined depends on the specific source and destination types and value. Floating-point to integer:

x: The fractional part is discarded toward zero.
If the truncated value cannot be represented in the destination integer type, behavior is undefined.
A NaN or infinity cannot be safely converted to an ordinary integer; check the domain and range before conversion. Integer to floating point:
The result may be exact or may be rounded to a nearby representable value.
float usually has less precision than double.
Integers larger than the exact precision range of the floating type may not retain every unit step. Signed to unsigned:
Conversion to an unsigned integer type is defined modulo the destination range size (maximum + 1).
A negative value therefore maps to a nonnegative value in that range. Unsigned to signed:
If the value is representable, it is preserved.

If it is not representable, the result is implementation-defined in C versions that specify that rule; consult the standard for the targeted version and implementation. Do not rely on a wraparound assumption. Character types:
char may be signed or unsigned depending on the implementation.
Use unsigned char for raw byte values when values 0 through UCHAR_MAX must be represented without negative interpretation.
Use the correct format specifier for printf.

b.x: For example, %d expects int, %u expects unsigned int, %f expects double for printf, and %lf is accepted by printf as equivalent to %f for double; in scanf, %f expects float * and %lf expects double *. Variadic format mismatches can cause undefined behavior, so check format specifiers carefully. A cast should be accompanied by a design reason.

If a program receives a value from an external source, validate its range before converting it to a narrow type. If the value represents money, measurements, or scientific data, choose a representation appropriate to the precision and rounding needs.

sec.t: Conversions in Conditions and Function Calls
sec.s: A condition accepts a scalar expression.

b.x: A condition accepts a scalar expression. Values that compare equal to zero are false; nonzero values are true. This is an implicit conversion to the truth value used by the control statement.

This executes because ready is nonzero. It is often clearer to write “if (ready != 0)” if the variable is an integer status, or use a Boolean variable with a meaningful name. Function calls can convert arguments to parameter types. For a function with a prototype, arguments are converted as if by assignment to the corresponding parameter type, with relevant language rules.

For variadic functions such as printf, default argument promotions apply to arguments after the fixed parameters. For example, float arguments are promoted to double in a variadic call, and narrow integer types undergo integer promotions. A function returning a value can also undergo conversion when that value is returned to the caller or stored in a destination.

Always read function prototypes and use compatible types. Compiler warnings about conversions often reveal bugs before the program runs. =================================================================
